eras.title: Key Topic 2: Hitler’s Rise to Power, 1919–33
Key Topic 3: Nazi Control and Dictatorship, 1933–39
Key Topic 4: Life in Nazi Germany, 1933–39

milestones.title: Kiel Naval Mutiny, Abdication of the Kaiser & The Armistice
milestones.specTag: KT 1.1 • End of the War, Revolution & Birth of the Republic
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did defeat in November 1918 create the Weimar Republic—and stain it from birth?
milestones.imageCaption: Allied commanders led by Marshal Foch confronting the German armistice delegation at Compiègne on 11 November 1918.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The Allied naval blockade, 3 November 1918 Kiel Mutiny, urban workers' councils, and the Compiègne Armistice.
milestones.catalyst: Four years of the British **Allied naval blockade** caused **Turnip Winter starvation** (~750,000 civilian deaths) and military collapse; when admirals ordered a final fleet sortie, **40,000 sailors mutinied at Kiel** on 3 November 1918.
milestones.turningPoint: Strikes and workers' councils forced **Kaiser Wilhelm II's abdication (9 Nov)**; **Philipp Scheidemann** proclaimed a Republic, **Friedrich Ebert** struck the **Ebert-Groener Pact** with the army, and **Matthias Erzberger** signed the **Armistice (11 Nov 1918)**.
milestones.impact: Averted Bolshevik civil war and ended First World War slaughter, yet historians debate whether Ebert's pact saved democracy or preserved anti-republican generals who branded democrats **'November Criminals'**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Before delegates could draft a democratic constitution, radical Communists rose in Berlin in January 1919 to replace Ebert's republic with Soviet councils.

keyTerms.definition: Naval uprising against a suicidal fleet battle order that sparked workers' and soldiers' councils across German cities.
10 November 1918 deal in which General Groener pledged army backing against communism if Ebert left the officer corps unpurged.
Ceasefire signed at Compiègne ending First World War fighting while leaving Weimar politicians to take the blame for defeat.

milestones.title: The Spartacist Uprising & Freikorps Repression in Berlin
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2 • Left-Wing Armed Challenge to the Republic
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Ebert rely on right-wing Freikorps paramilitaries to crush the Spartacists?
milestones.imageCaption: Armed Spartacist workers marching in Berlin during the January 1919 left-wing uprising against Ebert's government.
milestones.catalyst: Radical Communists in the **Spartacist League** led by **Rosa Luxemburg** and **Karl Liebknecht** rejected Ebert's moderate parliamentary republic and demanded rule by workers' and soldiers' councils.
milestones.turningPoint: In **January 1919**, **100,000 demonstrators** and armed Spartacists seized Berlin newspaper offices; Defence Minister Noske deployed **Freikorps** ex-soldier units who crushed the rising in bloody street fighting and murdered Luxemburg and Liebknecht.
milestones.impact: Enabled January 1919 National Assembly elections (83% turnout) to proceed at Weimar, yet permanently poisoned relations between **Social Democrats (SPD)** and **Communists (KPD)**—preventing a united left against Hitler in 1932–33.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Having survived left-wing revolt, the new Weimar coalition suffered a devastating nationalist blow at Paris in June 1919.

keyTerms.definition: Revolutionary German Communist movement led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht seeking a Soviet-style republic.
Fiercely nationalistic, anti-communist volunteer paramilitary units of demobilised ex-soldiers used by Ebert against left-wing risings.

milestones.title: The Treaty of Versailles & The ‘Stab in the Back’ Theory
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2 • Key Terms of Versailles & Early Unpopularity
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the Treaty of Versailles fuel nationalist hatred and the 'stab in the back' myth?
milestones.imageCaption: Right-wing nationalist Dolchstoßlegende ('Stab in the Back') poster depicting a civilian politician stabbing a German soldier from behind.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: German territorial losses (13% of European land), demilitarised Rhineland, Polish Corridor, and Ruhr industrial zone.
milestones.catalyst: Excluded from Allied talks at Paris and threatened with renewed invasion if Berlin refused, Weimar ministers had no choice on **28 June 1919** but to sign what Germans condemned as a **Diktat** (dictated peace).
milestones.turningPoint: Under **Article 231 (War Guilt)**, Germany accepted blame for the war, owed **£6.6 billion reparations** (set 1921), lost **13% of European land** and all colonies, demilitarised the **Rhineland**, and had its army capped at **100,000** with zero tanks, submarines, or air force.
milestones.impact: Became the sharpest cause of Weimar's early unpopularity: **Ludendorff** and **Hindenburg** promoted **the 'stab in the back' theory** (*Dolchstoßlegende*), claiming socialists and Jews had betrayed an undefeated army.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Six weeks after Versailles, Weimar delegates signed a remarkably democratic constitution—carrying two hidden structural time-bombs.

keyTerms.definition: Bitter German term for the dictated Versailles peace and its War Guilt clause justifying £6.6 billion in Allied reparations.
Right-wing nationalist myth claiming the German army was never beaten at the front but betrayed by 'November Criminals' at home.

milestones.title: The Weimar Constitution: Democratic Rights, PR & Article 48
milestones.specTag: KT 1.1 • Strengths & Weaknesses of the Weimar Constitution
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did proportional representation and Article 48 weaken an advanced democracy?
milestones.imageCaption: Elected delegates gathered at the Weimar National Assembly in 1919 to frame the Republic's democratic constitution.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The 18 federal states (Länder) of the Weimar Republic represented in the upper-house Reichsrat.
milestones.catalyst: Meeting safely away from Berlin street fighting in **Weimar**, the SPD-Centre-DDP coalition sought to replace autocratic Kaiser rule with Europe's most modern parliamentary democracy.
milestones.turningPoint: Signed on **11 August 1919**, the **Weimar Constitution** granted **universal suffrage at age 20** for men and women, free speech, and an elected President (7 years) and **Reichstag**—paired with pure **Proportional Representation (PR)** and **Article 48** presidential decree powers.
milestones.impact: Historians weigh its genuine democratic strengths against fatal institutional flaws: **PR** bred **29+ splinter parties** and fragile short-lived coalitions, while **Article 48** later enabled Brüning, Papen, and Hitler to bypass parliament legally.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Within six months of the constitution taking effect, a young army corporal in Munich helped launch a radical anti-Weimar nationalist programme.

keyTerms.definition: Voting system awarding 1 Reichstag seat per 60,000 votes, fair on paper but producing fragmented multi-party coalitions.
Emergency clause allowing the Reich President to suspend civil liberties and rule by decree without Reichstag approval.
The elected national parliament passing laws alongside the upper chamber representing Germany's 18 regional states (Länder).

milestones.title: Hitler Joins the DAP & Unveils the Twenty-Five Point Programme
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Hitler's Early Career & Setting Up the Nazi Party
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the February 1920 25-Point Programme blend nationalism, socialism, and antisemitism?
milestones.imageCaption: Munich railway locksmith Anton Drexler, founder of the German Workers' Party (DAP) joined by Adolf Hitler in September 1919.
milestones.catalyst: Sent by army intelligence in **September 1919** to spy on fringe groups in Munich, **Adolf Hitler** attended a tiny beer-hall meeting of **Anton Drexler**'s **German Workers' Party (DAP)** and joined to take charge of propaganda.
milestones.turningPoint: On **24 February 1920** at Munich's Hofbräuhaus, Hitler and Drexler announced **the Twenty-Five Point Programme** and rebranded the party **NSDAP** with a **swastika** flag and the newspaper ***Völkischer Beobachter*** (Dec 1920).
milestones.impact: Broadened early Bavarian appeal by combining nationalist demands (scrapping Versailles, *Lebensraum*), populist worker pledges (pensions, profit-sharing), and **Point 4 racial antisemitism** stripping Jews of German citizenship.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Three weeks after the 25-Point Programme in Munich, furious Freikorps brigades marched directly into Berlin to overthrow Ebert's republic.

keyTerms.definition: Anton Drexler's German Workers' Party (1919), renamed the National Socialist German Workers' Party (Nazi Party) in 1920.
February 1920 Nazi manifesto demanding the abolition of Versailles, Greater Germany, state welfare, and stripping Jews of citizenship.
Munich newspaper purchased by the NSDAP in December 1920 as the official print voice of Nazi propaganda.

milestones.title: The Kapp Putsch & The Berlin Workers’ General Strike
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2 • Right-Wing Armed Challenge & Army Disloyalty
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the Reichswehr refuse to fire on Kapp's rebels—and how did workers save Weimar?
milestones.imageCaption: Berlin workers rallying in the 15 March 1920 general strike that paralysed the capital and defeated the right-wing Kapp Putsch.
milestones.catalyst: Ordered to disband **Freikorps** brigades to comply with Versailles's 100,000-man army cap, right-wing politician **Wolfgang Kapp** and General von Lüttwitz marched **5,000 Freikorps** into Berlin in **March 1920**.
milestones.turningPoint: Army chief **General von Seeckt** refused to defend Ebert (*'Reichswehr does not fire upon Reichswehr'*), forcing the cabinet to flee; Berlin **trade unions** called a **general strike** cutting water, gas, coal, and trams until Kapp fled after four days.
milestones.impact: Proved working-class Berliners would defend the Republic against military dictatorship, yet exposed judicial and army bias—followed by **350+ right-wing assassinations** including **Matthias Erzberger (1921)** and **Walther Rathenau (1922)**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Disbanded Freikorps brawlers in Bavaria soon flowed into Munich, where Hitler seized absolute control of the NSDAP and built his own private stormtrooper army.

keyTerms.definition: Failed right-wing Freikorps coup in Berlin defeated after four days by a massive trade-union general strike.
Secret right-wing nationalist terrorist group that assassinated Weimar ministers Matthias Erzberger (1921) and Walther Rathenau (1922).

milestones.title: Hitler’s Führerprinzip Takeover & Creation of the SA (Brownshirts)
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Hitler's Party Leadership & Role of the SA
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Hitler's oratory and Ernst Röhm's SA transform the early Nazi Party by 1922?
milestones.imageCaption: SA commander Ernst Röhm in Munich, who organised unemployed ex-soldiers and Freikorps into the Nazi Party's paramilitary Brownshirts.
milestones.catalyst: Hitler's electrifying beer-hall speeches grew NSDAP membership past 3,000, sparking a **July 1921** clash when founder **Anton Drexler** proposed merging with rival nationalist groups.
milestones.turningPoint: Threatening to resign, Hitler sidelined Drexler to enforce absolute personal obedience (**Führerprinzip**, July 1921) and in **August 1921** founded the **Sturmabteilung (SA / Brownshirts)** under **Ernst Röhm**.
milestones.impact: Gave Hitler unchecked dictatorship inside the NSDAP alongside thousands of uniformed ex-soldiers who guarded Nazi rallies, intimidated rivals, and violently disrupted Communist and SPD meetings across Bavaria.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Hitler's growing Bavarian movement got its golden insurrection opportunity in 1923 when French troops invaded the Ruhr and destroyed the German currency.

keyTerms.definition: The 'Leadership Principle' abolishing internal party voting and giving Hitler unquestioned personal command over the NSDAP.
Nazi paramilitary 'Brownshirts' established in August 1921 under Ernst Röhm to protect Nazi speakers and beat up left-wing opponents.

milestones.title: French Occupation of the Ruhr & The 1923 Hyperinflation Catastrophe
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2 • Reasons for & Effects of Ruhr Occupation & Hyperinflation
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did passive resistance in the Ruhr trigger runaway hyperinflation across Germany?
milestones.imageCaption: Berlin shoppers carrying bundles of depreciated million-mark banknotes during the autumn 1923 hyperinflation crisis.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The January 1923 Franco-Belgian occupation of Germany's industrial Ruhr heartland.
milestones.catalyst: When Weimar defaulted on coal and timber **reparations**, **60,000 French and Belgian troops** occupied the industrial **Ruhr** in **January 1923** to seize factories and mines handling 80% of German coal and steel.
milestones.turningPoint: Chancellor Cuno ordered **passive resistance** strikes and printed trillions of unbacked paper marks to pay idle workers while tax revenues collapsed—driving the price of one loaf of bread to **201 billion marks** by November 1923.
milestones.impact: While debtors and speculators paid off loans effortlessly, **middle-class (*Mittelstand*) life savings** and elderly fixed pensions vanished overnight, permanently alienating millions of savers from Weimar democracy.
milestones.bridgeToNext: When new Chancellor Gustav Stresemann called off passive resistance in autumn 1923, furious nationalists in Munich backed Hitler's armed bid to seize power.

keyTerms.definition: Invasion of Germany's industrial Ruhr valley by 60,000 French and Belgian soldiers after Germany missed reparations deliveries.
Weimar-backed strike by Ruhr miners and rail workers funded by printing paper money, triggering catastrophic hyperinflation.
Runaway currency collapse making paper marks worthless (201bn marks for a loaf) and wiping out middle-class savings and pensions.

milestones.title: The Munich Beer Hall Putsch: Failure in the Streets
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2 • Reasons for & Events of the Munich Putsch (Nov 1923)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Hitler launch the November 1923 Munich Putsch—and why did it collapse in 24 hours?
milestones.imageCaption: Armed Nazi putschists manning a Munich street barricade during the failed Beer Hall Putsch of 8–9 November 1923.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Route of the 8–9 November 1923 Munich Putsch, Landsberg Fortress, and subsequent NSDAP Gau network.
milestones.catalyst: Inspired by **Mussolini's 1922 March on Rome**, 55,000 NSDAP members, and nationalist fury at Stresemann calling off Ruhr resistance, Hitler enlisted war hero **General Erich Ludendorff** for a coup.
milestones.turningPoint: On **8 November 1923**, Hitler and **600 SA men** stormed Munich's **Bürgerbräukeller** to coerce Bavarian leaders **Kahr, Lossow, and Seisser** at gunpoint; once released by Ludendorff, Kahr alerted police who shot **16 Nazis** dead on 9 November.
milestones.impact: Short-term disaster—Hitler was arrested, the **NSDAP was banned**, and armed rebellion failed—yet Q3d interpretations stress it forced Hitler onto the far deadlier **constitutional path** to power.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Just days after Hitler's arrest, Gustav Stresemann stabilised Germany's currency and secured American loans that transformed Weimar's fortunes.

keyTerms.definition: Hitler and Ludendorff's failed armed attempt to seize Bavaria at the Bürgerbräukeller and march on Berlin.
State Commissioner Gustav von Kahr, Army Commander Lossow, and Police Chief Seisser, who repudiated their coerced gunpoint support.

milestones.title: Stresemann’s Economic Stabilization: The Rentenmark & Dawes Plan
milestones.specTag: KT 1.3 • Causes of Economic Recovery (1924–29)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Stresemann's Rentenmark and the 1924 Dawes Plan end hyperinflation—and at what risk?
milestones.imageCaption: Founding board of the Deutsche Rentenbank (1923) convened under Gustav Stresemann to replace worthless paper marks.
milestones.catalyst: Appointed Chancellor in August 1923 at the peak of hyperinflation, **Gustav Stresemann** ended Ruhr passive resistance and slashed state spending to restore fiscal credibility.
milestones.turningPoint: Stresemann introduced the land-backed **Rentenmark (Nov 1923)**—converted into the gold-backed **Reichsmark (1924)**—and negotiated the **August 1924 Dawes Plan**: affordable staged reparations, French Ruhr withdrawal, and **800m gold marks** in US loans.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Genuine Recovery** points to doubled industrial output by 1928 and ended inflation, whereas the **'Dancing on a Volcano'** view stresses total dependence on recallable short-term **American loans and investment**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: While Stresemann stabilised the mark in 1924, sympathetic Munich judges turned Hitler's treason trial and prison stay into a national launchpad.

keyTerms.definition: Temporary land-backed currency (Nov 1923) and permanent gold-backed currency (1924) introduced under Stresemann to halt hyperinflation.
US-brokered pact scaling annual reparations to German capacity and injecting 800 million gold marks in Wall Street loans.

milestones.title: Hitler’s Treason Trial, Landsberg Prison & Mein Kampf
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2 • Consequences of the Munich Putsch & Nazi Ideology
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Hitler turn his 1924 trial and Landsberg imprisonment into a political triumph?
milestones.imageCaption: Adolf Hitler (left) with deputy Rudolf Hess and fellow putschists inside comfortable rooms at Landsberg Fortress in 1924.
milestones.catalyst: Tried for high treason in **February 1924**, Hitler benefited from right-wing judges who let him deliver front-page nationalist speeches attacking Weimar's 'November Criminals'.
milestones.turningPoint: Acquitting Ludendorff, judges gave Hitler the minimum **five-year sentence**, of which he served **barely nine months** at **Landsberg Fortress**, dictating ***Mein Kampf* ('My Struggle')** to **Rudolf Hess** before release in December 1924.
milestones.impact: Transformed Hitler from a regional Bavarian hothead into a **national right-wing figure**, codified core Nazi beliefs (**Aryan supremacy**, antisemitism, *Lebensraum*, *Führerprinzip*), and pivoted the NSDAP to **winning Reichstag elections legally**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Released into a prospering Weimar Republic, Hitler found voters far more impressed by Foreign Minister Stresemann's international breakthroughs of 1925–26.

keyTerms.definition: Hitler's 1924 ideological book dictated in Landsberg setting out Aryan racial supremacy, antisemitism, anti-communism, and Lebensraum.
Hitler's foreign-policy goal of conquering land in Eastern Europe and Russia to feed and settle an expanded Aryan population.

milestones.title: Stresemann Abroad: The Locarno Pact & League of Nations Council
milestones.specTag: KT 1.3 • Gaining International Acceptance Abroad
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the Locarno Pact and League of Nations entry restore Germany's status?
milestones.imageCaption: Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann arriving in Geneva as Germany joined the League of Nations in September 1926.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Stresemann's foreign-policy recovery—guaranteed western borders under Locarno (1925) and staged Allied Rhineland evacuation.
milestones.catalyst: Foreign Minister **Gustav Stresemann** pursued *Erfüllungspolitik* (fulfilment), calculating that peaceful Western cooperation was the surest way to end post-1919 diplomatic isolation and revise Versailles.
milestones.turningPoint: Voluntarily signing the **Locarno Pact (Oct 1925)**, Germany guaranteed its western borders with France and Belgium and Rhineland demilitarisation; in **September 1926**, Germany entered the **League of Nations** with a permanent Council seat.
milestones.impact: Won Stresemann the **1926 Nobel Peace Prize**, ended Allied occupation of Cologne, and bolstered moderate Weimar coalitions (plus Hindenburg's calm 1925 presidency)—even as nationalists attacked Locarno for accepting Versailles borders.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Shut out of mainstream voters' favour during Stresemann's 'Golden Years', Hitler spent 1925–28 quietly building a disciplined national party machine.

keyTerms.definition: Voluntary treaty with Britain, France, Belgium, and Italy accepting Germany's western borders and barring future Ruhr invasions.
International peacekeeping body in Geneva that admitted Germany with a permanent Council seat, restoring great-power status.

milestones.title: Nazi Party Reorganisation, The Bamberg Conference & 2.6% in 1928
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2 • Limited Nazi Support & Party Reorganisation (1924–28)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the Nazis win only 2.6% in May 1928 despite nationwide reorganisation?
milestones.imageCaption: Studio sequence by Heinrich Hoffmann (1927) showing Adolf Hitler rehearsing dramatic oratorical gestures during the 'Lean Years'.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Nationwide reorganisation of the NSDAP into regional Gaue after the February 1926 Bamberg Conference.
milestones.catalyst: Re-founding the NSDAP in February 1925, Hitler faced northern Nazis led by **Gregor Strasser** and **Joseph Goebbels** demanding socialist land and factory nationalisation.
milestones.turningPoint: At the **February 1926 Bamberg Conference**, Hitler crushed socialist dissent, won Goebbels over as Berlin *Gauleiter*, created 35 regional **Gaue**, founded the elite **SS**, and expanded youth/women's leagues—yet won just **12 seats (2.6%) in May 1928**.
milestones.impact: Stresemann-era stability kept extremists on the margins (SPD won 153 seats in 1928), yet historians stress Hitler's **100,000+ disciplined members** and rural shift built a ready-made national machine awaiting an economic crisis.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Meanwhile across Weimar cities between 1924 and 1929, rising wages, emancipated 'New Women', and avant-garde art sparked both pride and conservative anger.

keyTerms.definition: Party summit where Hitler defeated Gregor Strasser's socialist wing, reasserted the 25 Points, and won Joseph Goebbels's loyalty.
Regional Nazi Party leader appointed directly by Hitler to run one of Germany's electoral districts (Gaue).

milestones.title: Weimar Society: Living Standards, The ‘New Woman’ & Modernist Culture
milestones.specTag: KT 1.4 • Standard of Living, Women & Cultural Changes (1924–29)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How far did living standards, women's lives, and culture genuinely transform Weimar Germany?
milestones.imageCaption: Walter Gropius's glass-and-steel Bauhaus school at Dessau (1925–26), icon of Weimar modernist architecture.
milestones.catalyst: Industrial recovery, Article 109 gender equality, and lifting imperial censorship unleashed social welfare reforms and bold modernist experimentation across 1920s cities.
milestones.turningPoint: Real wages rose **10–25%**, **2m+ new homes** were built, and the **1927 Unemployment Insurance Act** covered 17m workers; urban **'New Women'** voted, served as MPs, and entered professions alongside **Walter Gropius's Bauhaus**, **Otto Dix / George Grosz** (*New Objectivity*), and **Fritz Lang's *Metropolis***.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Progressive Golden Era** highlights European leadership in welfare, female rights, and cinema, whereas **Deep Polarisation** stresses indebted farmers, persistent gender pay gaps, and rural outrage against 'degenerate' Berlin cabaret.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Weeks after negotiating the 1929 Young Plan, Stresemann died—and days later, the Wall Street Crash shattered Weimar's loan-funded prosperity.

keyTerms.definition: Welfare law requiring workers and employers to fund national unemployment and sickness benefits for 17 million workers.
Independent, voting, wage-earning young urban women of 1920s Weimar who wore bobbed hair, shorter skirts, and visited cafés freely.
Gropius's functionalist architecture school and gritty realist art (Dix, Grosz) exposing wartime trauma and social inequality.

milestones.title: Kellogg-Briand, The Young Plan & The October 1929 Wall Street Crash
milestones.specTag: KT 1.3 & KT 2.3 • End of Recovery & Onset of the Great Depression
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the October 1929 Wall Street Crash expose Weimar's reliance on US loans?
milestones.imageCaption: Crowds gathered outside the New York Stock Exchange in October 1929 as the Wall Street Crash triggered global loan recalls.
milestones.catalyst: After signing the **1928 Kellogg-Briand Pact**, Stresemann agreed the **1929 Young Plan** cutting reparations to **£2bn** over 59 years—giving Hitler national publicity alongside press baron Alfred Hugenberg's anti-Young Plan campaign.
milestones.turningPoint: When New York shares collapsed in the **October 1929 Wall Street Crash**, panicked American banks immediately recalled short-term **Dawes Plan loans**, bankrupting **50,000 German businesses**, shutting major banks, and slashing industrial output by **40%**.
milestones.impact: Confirmed Stresemann's warning that Germany was *'dancing on a volcano'*, shattering the Grand Coalition over unemployment pay in March 1930 and opening the door to political extremism.
milestones.bridgeToNext: As factories closed and soup queues lengthened, Chancellor Brüning's harsh austerity and Article 48 decrees drove millions toward Communists and Nazis.

keyTerms.definition: Final reparations deal cutting Germany's bill from £6.6bn to £2bn until 1988 and securing early Allied Rhineland withdrawal.
US stock-market collapse that prompted American banks to recall German loans, triggering mass bankruptcy and depression.

milestones.title: 6 Million Unemployed, Brüning’s Decrees & The July 1932 Nazi Surge
milestones.specTag: KT 2.3 • Growth of Unemployment, KPD & Nazi Support (1929–32)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the Great Depression make the Nazis Germany's largest party by July 1932?
milestones.imageCaption: Adolf Hitler addressing mass crowds with Joseph Goebbels in Berlin during the 1932 election campaigns.
milestones.catalyst: Registered unemployment hit **6 million** by winter 1932 while **'Hunger Chancellor' Heinrich Brüning** cut wages and dole benefits via **Article 48 decrees**, driving desperate workers to the **Communist Party (KPD, 100 seats)**.
milestones.turningPoint: **Joseph Goebbels** ran modern **'Work and Bread'** poster, radio, and **'Hitler over Germany'** flight campaigns while **400,000 SA men** fought KPD street battles; Nazi support surged from **107 seats (1930)** to **230 seats (37.3%) in July 1932**.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Structural Economic Despair** stresses mass unemployment, KPD fear among middle-class *Mittelstand*/industrialists (Thyssen), and Weimar failure, whereas **Hitler & Propaganda** highlights flexible Nazi cross-class appeal and charisma.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Despite holding 230 seats, Hindenburg despised the 'vulgar corporal'—forcing conservative elites into reckless backroom manoeuvres in late 1932.

keyTerms.definition: Centre Party Chancellor (1930–32) whose wage/welfare cuts and reliance on Article 48 decrees deepened misery and sidelined parliament.
Goebbels's simple, high-impact Nazi campaign slogan promising jobs for workers alongside protection from Communism for the middle class.

milestones.title: Papen, Schleicher, Hindenburg & Hitler’s Appointment as Chancellor
milestones.specTag: KT 2.4 • Causes of Hitler Becoming Chancellor (Jan 1933)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Hindenburg and Franz von Papen hand Hitler the Chancellorship when Nazi votes were falling?
milestones.imageCaption: SA stormtroopers marching in a torchlight parade through Berlin's Brandenburg Gate on the night of 30 January 1933.
milestones.catalyst: Although the Nazis **lost 2 million votes (falling to 196 seats)** in **November 1932** and neared bankruptcy, neither **Franz von Papen**'s 'Cabinet of Barons' nor **General Kurt von Schleicher** (Dec 1932) could command a Reichstag majority.
milestones.turningPoint: Plotting revenge on Schleicher, **Papen** met Hitler secretly on **4 January 1933** and persuaded **President Hindenburg** that a cabinet with **only 3 Nazis out of 11 ministers** would let conservatives *'push Hitler into a corner until he squeaked'*; Hitler became **Chancellor on 30 January 1933**.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Backstairs Elite Intrigue** stresses Papen and Hindenburg rescued a fading NSDAP through arrogance, whereas **Mass Movement Power** argues no right-wing government could rule without Hitler's 196-seat bloc.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Far from being tamed by Papen, Hitler called fresh March elections—and within four weeks a dramatic blaze in Berlin handed him emergency powers.

keyTerms.definition: January 1933 secret deal brokered by Franz von Papen, Oskar von Hindenburg, and industrialists persuading President Hindenburg to appoint Hitler.
Unelected conservative government led by Papen in 1932 that governed solely via Hindenburg's Article 48 decrees.

milestones.title: The Reichstag Fire, Enabling Act & One-Party Gleichschaltung
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1 • Destroying Democracy, Parties & Trade Unions (1933)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Hitler exploit the Reichstag Fire and Enabling Act to destroy Weimar democracy?
milestones.imageCaption: Adolf Hitler addressing Reichstag deputies beneath a giant swastika at the Kroll Opera House during passage of the Enabling Act, 23 March 1933.
milestones.catalyst: On **27 February 1933**, Dutch Communist **Marinus van der Lubbe** was caught inside the burning **Reichstag**; Hitler and Göring blamed a Communist plot to secure Hindenburg's **28 February Decree** suspending civil rights and jailing **4,000+ Communists**.
milestones.turningPoint: Winning **43.9%** in March 1933, Hitler barred 81 KPD deputies, promised Catholic Centre protection, and used SA intimidation at the **Kroll Opera House (23 March 1933)** to pass the **Enabling Act (444–94)**—smashing **trade unions (May)** and **banning all other parties (July)**.
milestones.impact: Legally dismantled the Weimar Constitution from within: Hitler could now enact laws for four years without Reichstag or Presidential consent, establishing a one-party totalitarian state.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Even as political opposition vanished in spring 1933, the new regime immediately launched ideological policies to reshape women's lives and marriage.

keyTerms.definition: Article 48 emergency decree suspending free speech, press, assembly, and trial rights—remained the legal basis of Nazi police rule.
Constitutional amendment giving Hitler's cabinet power to pass laws without the Reichstag for four years.
Nazi 'coordination' bringing regional states (Länder), trade unions, civil service, and political life under one-party control.

milestones.title: Kinder, Küche, Kirche, Marriage Loans, Mother’s Cross & Labour Reversal
milestones.specTag: KT 4.1 • Nazi Views & Policies on Women, Family, Work & Appearance
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How successful were Nazi policies aimed at reshaping women's family roles and employment?
milestones.imageCaption: The Cross of Honour of the German Mother (Mutterkreuz), awarded in bronze (4 children), silver (6), and gold (8+).
milestones.catalyst: Alarmed by falling birth rates and Weimar's emancipated 'New Woman', Nazi ideology under **Gertrud Scholtz-Klink** preached ***Kinder, Küche, Kirche*** alongside unpainted faces, braided hair, and traditional dress.
milestones.turningPoint: Women were sacked from legal/medical/civil posts (universities capped at 10%), offered **1,000-mark Marriage Loans (June 1933)** cancelled by 25% per child, honoured via the **Mother's Cross** and SS **Lebensborn** clinics (1935)—before **rearmament labour shortages (1937–39)** forced wives back into factories.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Ideological Impact** notes German births rose from 970,000 (1933) to 1.4m (1939), whereas **Pragmatic Failure** stresses average family size stayed near two children and female workers rose from **11.6m to 14.6m** by 1939.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Alongside reshaping family life in summer 1933, Hitler moved to bring Germany's Catholic and Protestant Churches under state control.

keyTerms.definition: 'Children, Kitchen, Church'—slogan summarising Nazi belief that Aryan women belonged in motherhood and homemaking.
Interest-free 1,000-mark vouchers for newlywed Aryan couples if the bride left work, with 25% written off for each child born.
State medals rewarding mothers of 4, 6, or 8+ children alongside Himmler's SS maternity homes for 'racially pure' births.

milestones.title: Controlling the Churches: The Catholic Concordat & Protestant Reich Church
milestones.specTag: KT 3.3 • Nazi Attempts to Control the Catholic & Protestant Churches
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Hitler try to subordinate Germany's Catholic and Protestant Churches?
milestones.imageCaption: Adolf Hitler greeting Reich Bishop Ludwig Müller in September 1934 during the campaign to build a Nazified Protestant Reich Church.
milestones.catalyst: Nearly all Germans belonged to either the **Protestant (two-thirds)** or **Catholic (one-third)** Church, whose Christian teachings of universal love and loyalty to God rivalled Nazi racial obedience.
milestones.turningPoint: Hitler signed the **July 1933 Concordat** with **Pope Pius XI** (trading Centre Party dissolution for promised Catholic school/youth freedom, soon broken by closing leagues and arresting priests) and merged Protestants into a Nazified **Reich Church** under **Ludwig Müller**.
milestones.impact: While 'German Christians' displayed swastikas beside altars and sacked Jewish-born pastors, **Pastor Martin Niemöller** and **Dietrich Bonhoeffer** founded the breakaway **Confessing Church (May 1934)**, proving Nazi ideological control over faith stayed incomplete.
milestones.bridgeToNext: By summer 1934, a far more immediate threat to Hitler's power erupted inside his own three-million-strong SA Brownshirts.

keyTerms.definition: Treaty with the Vatican guaranteeing Catholic schools and youth groups if clergy stayed out of politics—rapidly violated by Hitler.
Unified Protestant state church led by Reich Bishop Ludwig Müller and 'German Christians' blending Christianity with Nazi racism.
Breakaway Protestant church co-founded by Pastor Niemöller and Bonhoeffer rejecting Nazi interference in Christian doctrine.

milestones.shortTitle: Night of the Long Knives & Oath
milestones.title: Night of the Long Knives, Death of Hindenburg & The Army Oath
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1 • Crushing the SA Threat & Becoming Führer (1934)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did purging Ernst Röhm and Hindenburg's death complete Hitler's dictatorship in August 1934?
milestones.imageCaption: Adolf Hitler standing beside SA Chief of Staff Ernst Röhm in 1933, ten months before ordering Röhm's execution.
milestones.catalyst: **Ernst Röhm**'s **3 million SA stormtroopers** demanded a socialist 'Second Revolution' and merger with the 100,000-man army, prompting Reichswehr generals and **President Hindenburg** to threaten martial law unless Hitler curbed the SA.
milestones.turningPoint: On **30 June 1934** (**Night of the Long Knives**), **Himmler's SS** murdered **~400 rivals** including Röhm, Schleicher, and Gregor Strasser; when **Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934**, Hitler merged Chancellor and President as **Führer** and took a personal **army oath of allegiance**.
milestones.impact: Eliminated the last internal party rivals, elevated the **SS** above the tamed SA, legalised political murder, and bound every German soldier by personal honour to obey Adolf Hitler unconditionally.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Backed by the army and unchecked by any president, Heinrich Himmler and Reinhard Heydrich expanded a nationwide machinery of police terror and courts.

keyTerms.definition: 30 June 1934 SS purge executing Ernst Röhm, senior SA commanders, and political rivals to win regular army loyalty.
Hitler's merger of President and Chancellor upon Hindenburg's death, backed by an unconditional personal military oath of loyalty.

milestones.title: Himmler’s Police State: SS, Gestapo, Concentration Camps & People’s Court
milestones.specTag: KT 3.2 • Terror Apparatus & Nazi Control of the Legal System
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did a relatively small Gestapo force and Nazi courts paralyse open opposition?
milestones.imageCaption: Gestapo Headquarters at Prinz-Albrecht-Straße 8 in Berlin, nerve centre of secret-police surveillance and protective custody.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Pre-1939 Nazi concentration camps (Dachau, Sachsenhausen, Buchenwald) and SS/Gestapo control across Germany.
milestones.catalyst: To enforce *Gleichschaltung* across 70 million citizens, Hitler placed all German police forces under **Heinrich Himmler** (240,000-strong **SS**) and intelligence chief **Reinhard Heydrich** (**SD** and **Gestapo**).
milestones.turningPoint: Operating above the law via **protective custody**, **~30,000 Gestapo agents** relied on neighbourly denunciations and local **Block Wardens** to send suspects without trial to **concentration camps** (**Dachau**, opened March 1933), while the **People's Court (1934)** tried treason without juries.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Omnipotent Police Terror** stresses camp fear and Nazified judges crushed dissent, whereas **Self-Policing Consent** highlights that ordinary citizens' voluntary tip-offs powered a tiny Gestapo staff.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Police terror soon enforced codified racial persecution against Jewish Germans and minority groups at the September 1935 Nuremberg Rally.

keyTerms.definition: Himmler's black-uniformed racial elite (SS), Heydrich's intelligence service (SD), and non-uniformed Secret State Police (Gestapo).
SS-run prisons starting with Dachau (March 1933) holding political opponents, 'asocials', and minorities in indefinite protective custody.
Secret Nazi political court created in 1934 without juries or appeal rights, handing down harsh treason death sentences.

milestones.title: Early Persecution of Minorities & The September 1935 Nuremberg Laws
milestones.specTag: KT 4.4 • Racial Beliefs, Minorities & Legal Persecution of Jews
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Nazi racial beliefs escalate from the 1933 shop boycott to the 1935 Nuremberg Laws?
milestones.imageCaption: Official 1935 Nuremberg Laws racial chart classifying individuals by the ancestry of their four grandparents.
milestones.catalyst: Driven by **Social Darwinism** and Aryan *Herrenvolk* ideology, the regime staged the **1 April 1933 boycott of Jewish shops**, purged Jewish civil servants, forcibly **sterilised ~400,000 disabled people** (July 1933 Law), and persecuted **Roma/Sinti**, **Slavs**, and **homosexuals** (Paragraph 175).
milestones.turningPoint: At the **September 1935** rally, Hitler enacted two **Nuremberg Laws**: the **Reich Citizenship Law** stripped Jewish people of German citizenship and voting rights, and the **Law for the Protection of German Blood** outlawed marriage or relations between Jews and Aryans.
milestones.impact: Codified antisemitism into permanent Reich statute defined by **grandparent ancestry** rather than religion, turning German Jews into stateless outsiders excluded legally from the *Volksgemeinschaft*.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Just eleven months after Nuremberg, Goebbels temporarily hid anti-Jewish signs in Berlin to dazzle foreign visitors at the 1936 Olympic Games.

keyTerms.definition: Twin racial statutes stripping German Jews of citizenship (Reich Citizenship Law) and banning Jewish-Aryan marriage (Blood Law).
July 1933 eugenics law under which Hereditary Health Courts forcibly sterilised ~400,000 citizens with disabilities or hereditary conditions.
Racial registration and municipal camp internment (e.g. Berlin-Marzahn 1936) of Roma/Sinti alongside camp arrest of gay men.

milestones.title: Goebbels’ Propaganda: Volksempfänger, Nuremberg Rallies, 1936 Olympics & Art
milestones.specTag: KT 3.3 • Censorship, Media, Rallies, Sport & Control of Culture
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Goebbels use radio, rallies, the 1936 Olympics, and cultural censorship to mould attitudes?
milestones.imageCaption: African American sprinter Jesse Owens winning four gold medals at the August 1936 Berlin Olympic Stadium.
milestones.catalyst: Appointed Propaganda Minister in March 1933, **Joseph Goebbels** knew terror needed mass persuasion, forcing all journalists, filmmakers, and artists into the seven-branch **Reich Chamber of Culture**.
milestones.turningPoint: Goebbels put cheap **Volksempfänger radios** into **70% of homes**, staged **Albert Speer**'s 'Cathedral of Light' **Nuremberg Rallies**, showcased a 100,000-seat stadium at the **August 1936 Berlin Olympics** (where **Jesse Owens** won 4 golds), burned books (1933), and mocked **Degenerate Art (1937)**.
milestones.impact: Projected dazzling national unity and order at home and abroad while banning Weimar modernism, jazz, and Jewish writers—reinforcing the **'Hitler Myth'** even when citizens grumbled at local Party bosses.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Simultaneously, Nazi economic planners mobilized German workers for rearmament while replacing lost union rights with state leisure schemes.

keyTerms.definition: Cheap 76-mark state-subsidised radio (in 70% of German homes by 1939) unable to pick up distant foreign broadcasts.
Compulsory Nazi body policing press, literature, art, music, theatre, radio, and cinema, barring Jews and modernists.
Nazi label for confiscated modernist Weimar artworks (Dix, Grosz, Bauhaus) ridiculed in Munich's 1937 exhibition.

milestones.title: Employment & Living Standards: RAD, Rearmament, Strength Through Joy & Beauty of Labour
milestones.specTag: KT 4.3 • Reducing Unemployment, DAF, KdF & Beauty of Labour
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Did Nazi economic policies genuinely improve living standards for ordinary German workers?
milestones.imageCaption: Presentation of the Strength Through Joy (KdF) 'People's Car' prototype in 1938—for which no saver ever received a car.
milestones.catalyst: Inheriting **6m unemployed**, Hitler abolished unions for **Robert Ley**'s **German Labour Front (DAF)**, made six-month **National Labour Service (RAD)** on **Autobahns** compulsory (1935), reintroduced **conscription (1.4m troops by 1939)**, and put **Hermann Göring** over the **1936 Four-Year Plan**.
milestones.turningPoint: Official unemployment plunged below **300,000** (aided by **Invisible Unemployment** omitting sacked Jews, married women, and RAD conscripts), while **Strength Through Joy (KdF)** offered cheap holidays/theatre and **Beauty of Labour (SdA)** upgraded factory canteens.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Worker Gains** notes secure jobs, national pride, and KdF trips, whereas **Exploitation & 'Guns before Butter'** highlights frozen wages, **49-hour weeks**, food shortages under **Autarky**, and zero delivered KdF cars.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Preparing Germany for war within four years also demanded total ideological and physical capture of the next generation in schools and youth leagues.

keyTerms.definition: Statistical manipulation hiding dismissed Jews, married women pushed out of work, RAD conscripts, and camp detainees from jobless totals.
DAF leisure branch providing subsidised holidays, cruises, theatre tickets, and the unfulfilled Volkswagen car-savings scheme.
DAF scheme improving factory lighting, washrooms, and canteens—often built unpaid by workers themselves in their spare time.

milestones.title: Nazi Control of the Young: Hitler Youth, League of German Maidens & Schools
milestones.specTag: KT 4.2 • Hitler Youth, League of German Maidens & Education
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the Nazis use schools and compulsory youth movements to indoctrinate young Germans?
milestones.imageCaption: Teenage girls of the League of German Maidens (Bund Deutscher Mädel) lined up in uniform in 1937.
milestones.catalyst: Believing *'he who owns the youth gains the future'*, Hitler banned rival Scout and church clubs while Education Minister **Bernhard Rust** purged Jewish/democratic teachers and enrolled **97% of teachers** in the **Nazi Teachers' League (NSLB)**.
milestones.turningPoint: School curricula taught **Eugenics / Race Studies**, military PE (15% of timetable), and biased history/maths, while Baldur von Schirach's **Hitler Youth** (boys: rifle drill, marches) and **League of German Maidens** (girls: gymnastics, cooking, racial motherhood) became compulsory (**1936 & March 1939 Laws**, 8m+ members).
milestones.impact: Created millions of devoted young Nazis willing to inform on hesitant parents or teachers, though relentless military drill after 1936 provoked growing boredom and teenage non-conformity.
milestones.bridgeToNext: That growing teenage resentment—alongside brave church pastors and underground workers—fuelled pockets of pre-war resistance between 1937 and 1939.

keyTerms.definition: Nazi boys' movement (ages 14–18, after Jungvolk) drilling teenagers in route marches, map-reading, rifle shooting, and loyalty to Hitler.
Bund Deutscher Mädel (BDM) for girls aged 14–18 training future Aryan mothers through gymnastics, domestic skills, and racial hygiene.
Organisation enrolling 97% of German teachers to enforce Nazi salutes, rewritten textbooks, and compulsory Eugenics lessons.

milestones.title: Conformity vs Resistance: Niemöller, Edelweiss Pirates & Swing Youth
milestones.specTag: KT 3.4 • Scale of Support; Church & Youth Opposition (1933–39)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did most Germans conform—and how did church leaders and youth groups resist?
milestones.imageCaption: Prison cell wall inscription inside Cologne's Gestapo headquarters recording defiance by young Rhineland dissidents.
milestones.catalyst: Falling unemployment, national pride (Rhineland/Austria), propaganda, and Gestapo fear meant most Germans conformed outwardly, limiting dissent to private grumbling while exiled SPD (*Sopade*) and KPD cells were broken.
milestones.turningPoint: In **1937**, **Pope Pius XI** smuggled ***Mit Brennender Sorge*** into Catholic pulpits and Gestapo arrested **Pastor Martin Niemöller** (+800 Confessing pastors); meanwhile working-class **Edelweiss Pirates** ambushed Hitler Youth patrols and middle-class **Swing Youth** danced to banned American jazz.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Courageous Moral Defiance** highlights religious and cultural limits to totalitarian control, whereas **Limited Political Threat** notes neither churches nor youth gangs came close to toppling Hitler (even lone carpenter **Georg Elser's Nov 1939 bomb** missed him by 13 minutes).
milestones.bridgeToNext: With domestic opposition contained and foreign appeasement emboldening the regime, Nazi antisemitism exploded into open nationwide terror in November 1938.

keyTerms.definition: Papal encyclical ('With Burning Anxiety') by Pope Pius XI read secretly in German Catholic churches condemning Nazi racism and treaty breaches.
Working-class Rhineland teenagers wearing check shirts and edelweiss badges who camped freely, sang banned songs, and fought Hitler Youth patrols.
Affluent urban teenagers in Hamburg and Berlin who rejected Nazi militarism by wearing English fashion, welcoming Jews, and playing American swing.

milestones.title: Kristallnacht (‘Night of Broken Glass’), Aryanisation & Forced Emigration
milestones.specTag: KT 4.4 • Escalation of Anti-Jewish Persecution (1938–39)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Kristallnacht mark a violent turning point in Nazi persecution by September 1939?
milestones.imageCaption: A burning synagogue during the state-directed Kristallnacht pogrom of 9–10 November 1938 while fire brigades stood back.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Destroyed synagogues across the Reich during Kristallnacht (Nov 1938), camp round-ups of 30,000 Jewish men, and forced emigration.
milestones.catalyst: After young Polish Jew Herschel Grynszpan shot German diplomat Ernst vom Rath in Paris (Nov 1938), **Joseph Goebbels** and Hitler used his death to unleash nationwide state-sponsored violence.
milestones.turningPoint: On **9–10 November 1938 ('Kristallnacht')**, plainclothes SA and SS squads burned **1,000+ synagogues**, smashed **7,500 Jewish shops**, murdered **~100 Jews**, and sent **30,000 Jewish men** to Dachau, Buchenwald, and Sachsenhausen; Göring then fined Jews **1 billion marks** and completed forced **Aryanisation**.
milestones.impact: Shifted Nazi policy from legal discrimination to open physical terror and total economic exclusion—expelling Jewish children from state schools and driving **over half of Germany's Jews** into stripped, forced emigration via Heydrich's Reich Office before September 1939.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Twenty-one years after the 1918 Armistice, Weimar's democratic experiment had been replaced by a racial police dictatorship poised on the brink of European war in September 1939.

keyTerms.definition: State-orchestrated 'Night of Broken Glass' pogrom destroying synagogues and Jewish shops across Germany and Austria and arresting 30,000 men.
Forced seizure or rock-bottom transfer of Jewish-owned businesses, homes, and property to non-Jewish Germans, completed after Nov 1938.
Agency created under Reinhard Heydrich in early 1939 to force German and Austrian Jews to emigrate while confiscating their wealth.
